_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 02:13:38Z)**_

The run failed because the accepted gate was incompatible with its own containment environment—not because the macOS app failed to build.

| Check | Result | Actual cause |
|---|---|---|
| Release build | Passed | Xcode produced the app successfully. |
| 99-player network | Failed | The gate sandbox denied binding even to `127.0.0.1`: `PermissionError: Operation not permitted`. See [acceptance-progress.jsonl](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/runstate/task-0-d0f191c7/runs/328a4e34983e61be5dd45e22c9d453db/proofs/acceptance-progress.jsonl:5). |
| Visual comparison | Failed | The frozen verifier has malformed shell quoting. Bash reports a syntax error near line 118; the broken quote starts at [verify_macos_game.sh](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/jobs/aa49e5aa3f7a460bb574539472c8265d/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh:109). |

The network failure is deterministic: strict gate evaluation explicitly sets `allow_network: false` in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:4680), which becomes `(deny network*)` in [commands.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-sandbox/src/commands.rs:439). That denies the verifier’s loopback TCP server at [verify_macos_game.sh](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/jobs/aa49e5aa3f7a460bb574539472c8265d/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh:51). The visual check also downloads Nintendo artwork, so it would encounter the same no-network policy after its syntax error was fixed.

Why the agent claimed all checks passed: during turn 1 it edited the workspace copy of the verifier, fixed the quoting and replaced an obsolete macOS capture API. Its modified verifier passed build, the 99-client exchange, and visual comparison in [codex.out](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/runstate/task-0-d0f191c7/runs/328a4e34983e61be5dd45e22c9d453db/turns/turn-1/codex.out:75). But that modified file had hash `9e252c…`; the approved frozen verifier has hash `6155cf…`. DeadReckon correctly restores `.deadreckon` from trusted lifecycle state before the real gate in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:6523), so the gate evaluated the original broken verifier.

The UI’s “failed after turn 2” wording is slightly misleading. The gate actually ran after turn 1; turn 2 then produced no deliverable changes, so DeadReckon preserved the previous gate failure. The planner reconstructs the message using the final turn number in [plan.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/plan.rs:4130).

Current status: the screenshot’s run `d7524b52…` has now failed with the exact same two results. Attempt 3, `f515f013…`, started at 22:09:47 EDT and will encounter the same frozen blockers.

The proper correction is outside the child implementation:

- Fix and syntax-check the approved verifier.
- Replace the live Nintendo download with a pinned local fixture.
- Use ScreenCaptureKit instead of `CGWindowListCreateImage`.
- Either permit loopback networking for strict gates or redesign that check not to require TCP.
- Relaunch with a newly approved contract bundle.

I made no changes to the active plan or its files.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 02:19:17Z)**_

Yes. DeadReckon is close to supporting this, but the acceptance contract currently does not carry capability requirements into the gate.

Today:

- `AcceptanceCheck` describes only the command and cwd in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:140).
- The compiled contract has no capability field in [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:179).
- Job creation always starts from a networkless `workspace_only` policy in [job.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/job.rs:266).
- The gate independently hardcodes `allow_network: false` in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:4688).

The right design is to make capabilities an explicit, reviewable part of each done check:

```yaml
version: 2

checks:
  - name: Exercise 99 TCP clients
    kind: shell
    command: bash .deadreckon/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh network
    capabilities:
      network:
        loopback: true
        outbound: []

  - name: Compare the rendered window
    kind: shell
    command: bash .deadreckon/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh visual
    capabilities:
      network:
        loopback: false
        outbound: []
```

For external resources, I would avoid live gate networking and declare frozen inputs instead:

```yaml
fixtures:
  - name: tetris-99-reference
    url: https://assets.nintendo.com/example.png
    sha256: "sha256:..."
    destination: .deadreckon/acceptance/fixtures/tetris-99.png
```

The controller downloads and hashes that fixture before approval, displays it in the launch preview, and freezes it into the contract bundle. The gate remains deterministic and offline.

The capability flow should be:

1. The definition-of-done compiler proposes capabilities from the criteria.
2. The operator sees “gate network: loopback” or “external fixtures: 1” before accepting.
3. The approved capabilities are frozen into a new gate-specific section of `JobExecutionPolicy`.
4. The authority digest binds that policy, so it cannot silently escalate later.
5. Gate execution reads the frozen policy instead of hardcoding `allow_network: false`.
6. Each check runs with its minimum capability, and the signed marker records what was granted.

Automatic inference should propose authority, never silently grant it. For example, prose mentioning “99 TCP clients” can propose loopback; arbitrary shell invoking `curl` should fail preflight unless the contract explicitly declares outbound access or a frozen fixture.

For this particular contract, the safest MVP is:

- Add a distinct `loopback` gate capability.
- Keep arbitrary outbound gate networking prohibited.
- Freeze remote comparison assets before launch.
- Run `bash -n` on frozen shell helpers during preflight.
- Add backend tests proving loopback works while internet access remains denied.

That would have rejected this job before it spent any agent turns: one error for malformed Bash, one for undeclared loopback, and one for the unfrozen Nintendo download. No code was changed in this review.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 02:33:21Z)**_

The causal chain is now proven end to end:

- `acceptance.yaml` is compiled for review, but capabilities are currently discarded.
- `start` preserves that compiled contract through preview, confirmation, replay, and `LaunchPlan`.
- every durable launch route converges on `create_job`, which freezes the contract and hashes policy.
- graph drivers reuse the frozen contract for root plans, subplans, and child runs.
- provider permissions already have a frozen-policy projection path.
- strict completion breaks parity by hardcoding `allow_network: false`.

I also verified the macOS Seatbelt rule needed for loopback with an actual bind/connect probe. I’m moving into implementation with two explicit modes—`loopback` and `full`—and default-deny compatibility for all existing contracts.

More importantly, it tests only whether fake binaries exist, not whether DeadReckon can actually construct and run those providers.

The live audit has already found two concrete failures:

- `doctor` reports Gemini, OpenCode, Copilot, and Pi against the wrong `codex` binary.
- The provider registry rejects the installed Copilot 1.0.71 because it probes `copilot --help`; the current CLI’s reliable identity is from `copilot --version`.

I’m therefore not merging PR #2 directly. I’ve started a clean `codex/provider-conformance` branch and written failing tests that require doctor, provider listing, startup, and runtime to consume the same already-resolved provider executable—including config overrides. I’ve just added that executable to the runtime route object; next I’m wiring doctor and registry probes to it. After the deterministic tests pass, I’ll use the repository’s real-provider harness against all seven named CLI routes, using disposable evidence so we learn which providers genuinely complete a DeadReckon job rather than merely appearing installed.

_**User (2026-08-06 14:51:02Z)**_

can you explain how we've addressed this porblem and how we've approach implementation so as to not cause regressions from the 0.8.3 release

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 14:51:36Z)**_

We’ve addressed it by removing the guess, not by expanding the guess table.

Before this change there were two separate truths:

- Runtime built a provider through `ProviderRouter`, merging registry defaults, `providers.d` overrides, and the operator’s `config.toml`.
- `doctor` independently inspected raw TOML and guessed `claude` for names containing “claude,” otherwise `codex`.

That is why Pi was reported as Codex, and why similar drift could recur for Gemini, OpenCode, Copilot, or a custom binary override.

The implementation now follows one chain:

```text
registry descriptor + operator config
                ↓
       ProviderRouter constructs route
                ↓
 route exposes exact executable it will launch
                ↓
 startup / doctor / detect / providers check
 all inspect that same resolved executable
```

Concretely:

- Every CLI provider exposes its already-resolved executable through the existing runtime provider object.
- The existing shared startup setup resolver consumes that executable, so its provider-selection order and auth checks are unchanged.
- `doctor` now calls that startup resolver instead of parsing provider kinds and guessing binaries.
- `providers list`, `providers check`, and `detect` probe the executable runtime constructed, including a configured binary override.
- A descriptor-less custom CLI is now rejected by doctor if runtime would reject it; doctor can no longer claim a route is healthy merely because a similarly named executable exists.
- Copilot’s separate stale probe was corrected from `copilot --help` to the current, verified `copilot --version`.

The regression controls are deliberate:

- No startup phase ordering changed.
- No durable config, Job, LaunchPlan, acceptance, supervisor, or protocol schema changed.
- No default provider ordering changed.
- No preview path gained a process or auth probe.
- The new trait method defaults to `None`, so HTTP, scripted, and future providers remain behavior-compatible until they explicitly expose an executable.
- Tests pin all seven CLI routes, config overrides, invalid custom routes, startup auth behavior, provider listing, Copilot 1.0.71, and the real-provider harness.
- The full provider suite is green: 107 unit tests + 45 provider integration tests, plus setup, doctor, provider-list, release-harness, formatting, and strict Clippy checks.

One important honesty point: this branch descends from the hardened startup commit and the network-contract work, while `origin/main` has the separate `v0.8.3-rc.1` release-preparation commit. I have not yet claimed release-line compatibility. Before pushing this provider branch, I will replay these commits in a clean temporary worktree based on `origin/main` and run the same focused suite there. That clean reconciliation—not an assumption—is how we will prove the change does not regress 0.8.3.

_**User (2026-08-06 14:54:02Z)**_

how has our fix improved on the PR?

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 14:54:22Z)**_

Our fix improves on PR #2 by removing the underlying source of inconsistency, rather than adding a broader fallback.

| Concern | PR #2 | Our fix |
|---|---|---|
| Binary selection | Guesses from config, registry default, then provider name | Asks `ProviderRouter` for the exact executable it constructed |
| Startup | Resolves the provider independently | Uses the same resolved route and executable as runtime |
| Doctor | Maintains its own provider-name/binary logic | Calls the shared startup/runtime selection path |
| `providers list/check` | Can probe the descriptor default instead of an override | Probes the actual configured executable |
| Custom providers | May report a descriptor-less provider as healthy | Rejects it consistently with runtime |
| Copilot | Runs `copilot --help`, causing a false version failure | Runs `copilot --version`; detects 1.0.71 correctly |
| Coverage | Fake-binary tests around fallback behavior | Tests all seven CLI routes, overrides, custom-route rejection, and release-harness coverage |
| Real operation | Does not establish job completion | Extends the durable real-provider preflight to every named CLI provider |

The architectural change is:

```text
registry + descriptor + user config
                ↓
          ProviderRouter
                ↓
       resolved runtime route
       ├── exact executable
       ├── authentication policy
       └── concrete adapter
                ↓
 startup / doctor / list / check / execution
```

Previously, those consumers could independently reinterpret the provider name. That is why, for example, Gemini, OpenCode, Copilot, and Pi could be diagnosed through the Codex executable even though runtime would launch something different.

This also protects the 0.8.3 startup fixes:

- We have not changed startup phase ordering.
- We have not changed preview-mode or authentication policy.
- We have not added fields to durable jobs, `LaunchPlan`, or the execution protocol.
- Network authority still comes exclusively from the compiled done contract.
- The provider change only makes startup consume the executable already selected by the canonical runtime route.

The focused tests are passing, and a host-level probe now reports all seven CLI routes as ready. One distinction remains important: “binary and route are correctly resolved” is not yet the same as “every provider successfully completes and cancels a durable DeadReckon job.” The extended real-provider preflight is the next verification layer.

The implementation checkpoint is staged but not yet committed: the first commit attempt was stopped because the sandbox could not create `.git/index.lock`. No files were lost or partially committed.

_**User (2026-08-06 15:11:54Z)**_

can you explain how this happened?


• The Copilot evidence proves an important distinction the PR never saw: Copilot successfully
  edited the fixture and passed the signed deterministic gate, but the same route cannot perform
  DeadReckon’s schema-only semantic judgment. I’m now checking each CLI’s actual installed
  capability surface before deciding between two honest designs: native schema-only support
  where the CLI can prove it, or an explicit reviewer route recorded in the immutable launch
  plan where it cannot.

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 15:12:20Z)**_

This happened because a DeadReckon job has two distinct model-facing roles, but the direct-run launch plan recorded only one provider:

```text
Copilot as coder
      ↓
edits purpose.sh successfully
      ↓
deterministic acceptance check passes
      ↓
DeadReckon needs an independent semantic judgment
      ↓
no reviewer is recorded, so it falls back to Copilot
      ↓
Copilot route cannot prove schema-constrained judgment
      ↓
job becomes needs_review / semantic_unavailable
```

The important distinction is that Copilot’s `--output-format json` produces a JSON event envelope. It does not constrain the model’s answer to an arbitrary JSON Schema supplied by DeadReckon.

For ordinary coding, that is fine. DeadReckon parsed Copilot’s events, observed the file change, ran the frozen acceptance command, and created a signed passing gate marker.

For final semantic judgment, DeadReckon requires a stricter posture:

- read-only execution;
- tools disabled or otherwise provably unavailable;
- response constrained to DeadReckon’s judgment schema;
- response validated before it can authorize a verified result.

Claude and Codex have dedicated adapters that can establish this posture. The generic Copilot adapter cannot currently prove all of it, so it intentionally refuses before launching a second Copilot process. The evidence confirms this: the semantic phase consumed zero tokens and about 0.001 seconds.

Why did it try Copilot again? The direct `run --provider cli:copilot` path currently freezes only:

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "coder": "cli:copilot"
  }
}
```

The semantic router searches in this order:

1. reviewer
2. coder
3. planner
4. default child

Because no reviewer was recorded, it selected the coder—Copilot.

So this is not “Copilot failed to implement the task.” It is “Copilot succeeded as a worker, but the startup plan did not assign a provider capable of the separate verifier role.”

PR #2 could not reveal this because it tested only whether a guessed binary existed. Even our improved doctor proved only route resolution and credential readiness. The real durable preflight exposed the missing role-capability contract.

The safe fix is likely to record an explicit reviewer in the immutable launch plan for providers that cannot serve as strict semantic judges. That preserves the fail-closed semantic boundary instead of weakening it merely to make the route appear green.

---

_**User (2026-08-06 15:12:20Z)**_

and whether it was only for copilot or any other agent that deadreckon harnesses?

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 15:12:46Z)**_

It is not Copilot-specific. Copilot was simply the first generic provider to complete the coding work successfully enough to expose the next boundary.

| Provider route | Adapter | Can currently perform strict semantic judgment? | Current evidence |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `cli:claude-code` | Dedicated Claude adapter | Yes, when capability probe passes | Existing release proof |
| `cli:codex` | Dedicated Codex adapter | Yes, when capability probe passes | Existing release proof |
| `cli:codex-server` | Codex app-server | Yes; schema-only requests fall back to ephemeral Codex exec | Code and tests |
| `cli:copilot` | Generic CLI adapter | No | Observed after successful coding and gate |
| `cli:pi` | Generic CLI adapter | No | Guaranteed by the same code path, although its current run failed earlier with a provider-side `402 Insufficient Balance` |
| `cli:gemini` | Generic CLI adapter | No | Guaranteed by the same code path; current credentials also have an eligibility problem |
| `cli:opencode` | Generic CLI adapter | No | Guaranteed by the same code path; its structured event stream has additional unresolved ambiguity |
| `smoke` | Scripted fixture | Deliberately no | It is not an independent model judge |

The shared generic driver contains an unconditional refusal:

```rust
if request.output_schema.is_some() {
    return Err(
        "provider descriptor cannot prove schema-only structured-text posture"
    );
}
```

Therefore Gemini, OpenCode, Copilot, and Pi will all encounter the same semantic-verification failure if the job uses that provider as both coder and reviewer.

Their earlier behavior can differ:

- Copilot successfully implemented the change, so it reached the semantic boundary.
- Pi failed first because its selected upstream model returned `402 Insufficient Balance`.
- Gemini may fail first at account eligibility.
- OpenCode may fail first because its event output can contain an answer, an error, and `null` while still exiting zero.

But if those earlier problems are resolved, all four still reach the same generic schema refusal.

The limitation is role-specific, not a blanket statement that these providers cannot work with DeadReckon:

- They may be valid coding workers.
- They cannot currently be the strict semantic reviewer.
- A launch plan containing, for example, Copilot as coder and Codex as reviewer can preserve both capabilities safely.

Copilot was therefore the diagnostic canary, not the only affected provider.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 15:13:08Z)**_

I’m continuing with the role-safe design the evidence points to: preserve the generic providers’ fail-closed semantic boundary, expose an explicit reviewer on durable direct runs, freeze that reviewer into the launch plan, and make the real-provider proof record which route coded versus judged. I’ll use the existing `start --reviewer-provider` path as the in-repo working sibling so direct-run behavior matches startup rather than inventing a parallel selection rule.

The exact split is:

- `cli:copilot`, `cli:gemini`, `cli:opencode`, and `cli:pi` all use DeadReckon’s generic CLI adapter. That adapter deliberately rejects `output_schema`, so none of those routes can currently act as the strict semantic judge.
- Any custom descriptor-based CLI routed through that same generic adapter has the same limitation.
- `cli:claude-code` and `cli:codex` have dedicated, capability-probed schema-only implementations.
- `cli:codex-server` delegates schema-only/read-only review to the proven ephemeral Codex route.
- Anthropic/OpenAI HTTP routes express a JSON schema in their native request protocol; OpenAI-compatible endpoints still need live verification because protocol compatibility varies.
- `smoke` can exercise the transport, but deliberately returns “uncertain”; it is not independent proof.

Copilot exposed the problem first because its worker phase succeeded. With no explicit reviewer in the launch plan, the semantic router fell back from `reviewer` to `coder`, selected Copilot again, and then hit the generic adapter’s schema refusal. The same sequence would affect Gemini, OpenCode, or Pi after a successful coding turn.

The safe product change is therefore not a Copilot exception. It is to separate “worker route” from “semantic reviewer route,” freeze both in the immutable launch plan, and make generic CLI workers use an explicitly selected schema-capable reviewer. I’m implementing that at the shared direct-run/startup boundary so every affected provider gets the same behavior.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 16:10:43Z)**_

Current state: the network-aware done-contract fix is already committed and pushed, and the first provider-doctor correction is also committed. The broader provider-conformance work is still local and uncommitted because the full 0.8.3 graph regression suite found one genuine compatibility gap before I froze it.

What is working now:

- `run`, guided `start`, full-plan, review graphs, campaigns, forks, and replay all distinguish the implementation worker from the schema-capable final reviewer.
- Copilot, Gemini, OpenCode, Pi, and custom generic CLIs can be workers but can no longer silently claim schema-only review capability.
- Claude, Codex, Codex server, Anthropic/OpenAI routes, and the test smoke route can review natively.
- `doctor --live` performs a real bounded provider turn; ordinary doctor output explicitly says it is only a static setup probe.
- Pi and OpenCode error streams are now classified instead of being mistaken for successful zero-exit turns.
- Release proof schema 3 records and requires both worker and reviewer identities.

The full graph run passed 172/195 tests. The 23 failures split into:

- 18 old test fixtures using fake generic workers without declaring a reviewer—the new refusal is correct.
- 5 smoke/lifecycle failures caused by treating the scripted smoke judge like a generic CLI; that diagnosis is now fixed.
- The fixture failures exposed a real usability omission: only command-line reviewer flags were supported. I’m currently adding `defaults.reviewer_provider` and `defaults.reviewer_model`, so a configured generic worker has one durable reviewer policy across every startup/graph path and old stored plans can migrate safely.

Nothing from this unfinished semantic-review expansion has been committed or pushed yet. After the suite is green, I’ll commit it, replay it on the exact v0.8.3 baseline, run the real installed-provider matrix, then rebase and prepare—not publish—the 0.8.4 release.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 17:04:12Z)**_

The expanded evidence exposed a genuine product propagation bug, not a fixture problem: the root launch plan contains `reviewer=cli:codex`, but each delegated graph child is invoked with only its worker provider. This is one of the startup/graph touchpoints the narrower suites missed; I’m fixing the delegated child argv so it carries the reviewer route/model frozen in the parent plan.

Provider evidence so far:

- Copilot works as a worker and passed the deterministic signed gate, but its CLI cannot perform DeadReckon’s schema-constrained semantic review.
- The same limitation applies structurally to generic CLI routes such as Gemini, OpenCode, Pi, and custom CLIs—not only Copilot.
- Native semantic-review routes are Claude, Codex, codex-server, and the API adapter.
- Pi reached its external provider but received a billing `402`.
- The installed Gemini version was unsupported/ineligible.
- OpenCode failed on its installed capability/configuration surface.
- The real Claude/Codex/codex-server matrix remains to be completed.

Next sequence:

1. Add or confirm the saved-launch replay regression test.

6. Rebase the verified work onto current `main`.
7. Prepare the 0.8.4 release changes without tagging or publishing yet.

Unrelated documentation, SpecStory, design, and build-output changes remain excluded from this workstream.
